course: Linear Algebra - Vectors, Spaces and the SVD
attribution: Original scope and sequence authored for the Luminfest Learning Harness, dedicated to the public domain under CC0.
scope: Structure only: concept titles, unit order and prerequisite intent. No third-party curriculum text is reproduced, and no restricted source is ingested.
description: A one-semester linear algebra course: vectors, linear combinations and span; linear systems and Gaussian elimination; matrix algebra and inverses; vector spaces, independence and basis; the four fundamental subspaces and rank-nullity; linear transformations and change of basis; orthogonality, projection and Gram-Schmidt; least squares and QR; determinants; eigenvalues, diagonalisation and Markov chains; symmetric matrices and the spectral theorem; and the singular value decomposition with low-rank approximation.

concepts.title: Vectors as Ordered n-Tuples
concepts.summary: A vector in R^n is an ordered list of n real numbers, and two vectors are added componentwise while a scalar multiplies every component, so R^n is closed under both operations.

concepts.title: Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication
concepts.summary: Vector addition in R^n is commutative and associative with a zero vector and an additive inverse, and scalar multiplication distributes over both, so R^n satisfies the vector-space axioms before any abstraction.

concepts.title: Vectors as Arrows in R2 and R3
concepts.summary: In R^2 and R^3 a vector is drawn as an arrow from the origin, addition is the diagonal of the parallelogram its two arrows span, and a negative scalar reverses the arrow rather than only stretching it.

concepts.title: Linear Combinations of Vectors
concepts.summary: A linear combination of v1 to vk is c1v1 + ... + ckvk with real scalars, and it is defined only when all the vectors lie in the same R^n so the sum is taken componentwise.

concepts.title: The Span of a Set of Vectors
concepts.summary: The span of a set is the set of all its linear combinations, so it always contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, which makes it a subspace even when the set is not.

concepts.title: When a Set Spans R^n
concepts.summary: A set of vectors spans R^n exactly when the matrix with those vectors as columns has a pivot in every row, so more than n vectors can still fail to span while fewer than n never span.
prerequisites: The Span of a Set of Vectors

concepts.title: The Dot Product
concepts.summary: The dot product u.v is the sum of the products of corresponding components, it is symmetric and bilinear, and it is zero exactly when the two nonzero vectors are perpendicular.

concepts.title: Length, Distance, and Unit Vectors
concepts.summary: The length of v is the square root of v.v, which is zero only for the zero vector, and scaling by c multiplies length by the absolute value of c, so a unit vector is a nonzero vector divided by its own length.

concepts.title: Angles and the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
concepts.summary: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives |u.v| at most the product of the two lengths, so for nonzero vectors cos(theta) = u.v/(|u||v|) is defined and lies between -1 and 1, which makes the angle well defined.

concepts.title: Each Equation as a Hyperplane
concepts.summary: One linear equation in n unknowns is the solution set of a single row, a hyperplane of dimension n - 1, so a system of m equations asks for the common intersection of m such hyperplanes in R^n.

concepts.title: The Three Solution Cases
concepts.summary: A linear system has no solution, exactly one solution, or infinitely many, because once two distinct solutions exist the whole line through them consists of solutions, so a system can never have exactly two.

concepts.title: Homogeneous Systems and the Trivial Solution
concepts.summary: A homogeneous system Ax = 0 always has the trivial solution x = 0, so it is consistent for every matrix and is either uniquely trivial or has infinitely many solutions.

concepts.title: Augmented Matrices and Row Equivalence
concepts.summary: The augmented matrix records the coefficients and the right-hand side together, and two augmented matrices that are row equivalent have exactly the same solution set, so elimination can be performed on the matrix alone.

concepts.title: Elementary Row Operations
concepts.summary: Swapping two rows, adding a multiple of one row to another, and multiplying a row by a nonzero scalar each preserve the solution set, which is why the reduced system answers the original question.

concepts.title: Pivots and the Elimination Procedure
concepts.summary: Elimination takes the leftmost nonzero entry of the working row as pivot, clears every entry below it, and repeats on the submatrix, so it terminates in echelon form from which back substitution gives x.

concepts.title: Echelon Form and the Staircase
concepts.summary: A matrix is in echelon form when every nonzero row sits above the zero rows, each pivot lies to the right of the pivot above it, and all entries below a pivot are zero, so the pivots are found by scanning left to right.

concepts.title: Reduced Row Echelon Form and Pivot Columns
concepts.summary: Reduced echelon form further makes each pivot 1 and clears the entries above it, and that form is unique for a given matrix, so two matrices are row equivalent exactly when they reduce to the same matrix.

concepts.title: Free Variables and Parametric Solutions
concepts.summary: In reduced form every non-pivot column carries a free variable, so a consistent system with f free variables has a solution set described by f independent parameters and is a translate of an f-dimensional subspace.
prerequisites: Reduced Row Echelon Form and Pivot Columns

concepts.title: Particular Solution plus Null Space
concepts.summary: When Ax = b is consistent, its complete solution is x = xp + xn where xp is one particular solution and xn ranges over the null space of A, because differences of two solutions to Ax = b both solve Ax = 0.

concepts.title: Consistency and a Pivot in the Last Column
concepts.summary: The system Ax = b is consistent exactly when row reduction of the augmented matrix leaves no pivot in the last column, since such a pivot is the row 0 = c with c nonzero.

concepts.title: Matrix Addition and Scalar Multiplication
concepts.summary: Two matrices can be added only when they have the same shape, entry by entry, and a scalar multiplies every entry, so the m by n matrices form a vector space of dimension mn under those two operations.

concepts.title: The Matrix Product and Its Dimensions
concepts.summary: The product AB is defined only when the column count of A equals the row count of B, its ij entry is the dot product of row i of A with column j of B, and the product is generally not commutative.

concepts.title: Matrix Multiplication as Composition
concepts.summary: An m by n matrix A applied to an n by p matrix B represents B followed by A, which is why (AB)x = A(Bx) and why the product is associative while most matrices have no multiplicative inverse.
prerequisites: The Matrix Product and Its Dimensions

concepts.title: The Transpose and Its Rules
concepts.summary: The transpose swaps rows and columns, so the transpose of a transpose returns the original and the transpose of a product reverses the order, giving (AB)^T = B^T A^T.

concepts.title: Symmetric, Diagonal, and Triangular Matrices
concepts.summary: A matrix is symmetric when it equals its transpose, diagonal when only its diagonal entries may be nonzero, and triangular when one whole side of the diagonal vanishes, and each class is closed under addition but not in general under multiplication.

concepts.title: Invertibility and the Two-Sided Inverse
concepts.summary: An n by n matrix A is invertible when some B satisfies AB = BA = I, and then B is unique and written A inverse, which requires A to be square before the question can even be asked.

concepts.title: Inverses of Products and Transposes
concepts.summary: When both factors are invertible, (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1 and the inverse of a transpose is the transpose of the inverse, because undoing a composition undoes the last step first.

concepts.title: Solving Ax=b with an Inverse
concepts.summary: If A is invertible then Ax = b has the unique solution x = A^-1 b for every b, so invertibility is exactly the condition that the system is never inconsistent and never has a free variable.

concepts.title: Elementary Matrices and Row Operations
concepts.summary: Every elementary row operation is left multiplication by an elementary matrix obtained from the identity, and each such matrix is invertible with an elementary inverse, so elimination is a product of matrices.

concepts.title: The LU Factorization
concepts.summary: When elimination needs only row replacements, A factors as A = LU with L unit lower triangular holding the multipliers and U the echelon form, while any row swap is absorbed by a permutation so that PA = LU.

concepts.title: The Subspace Test
concepts.summary: A subset of R^n is a subspace exactly when it contains the zero vector and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication, so a plane through the origin qualifies while the same plane shifted off the origin does not.

concepts.title: Spans and Null Spaces as Subspaces
concepts.summary: The span of any set of vectors is a subspace, and the solution set of Ax = 0 is the span of the vectors attached to its free variables, whereas the solution set of Ax = b with b nonzero is not a subspace.

concepts.title: Independence as a Trivial Combination
concepts.summary: The vectors v1 to vk are linearly independent when c1v1 + ... + ckvk = 0 forces every coefficient to be zero, so a set is dependent exactly when one of its members is a combination of the others.

concepts.title: Pivots and Linear Independence
concepts.summary: The columns of a matrix are linearly independent exactly when every column is a pivot column, which is impossible when the matrix has more columns than rows, so such a set is always dependent.

concepts.title: Dependence and Redundant Vectors
concepts.summary: In a dependent set some vector is a combination of the vectors before it, so deleting it leaves the span unchanged, which is why a basis may contain no redundant vector.

concepts.title: The Basis Definition
concepts.summary: A basis of a subspace is a set that both spans the subspace and is linearly independent, so every vector of the subspace is a combination of the basis vectors in exactly one way.

concepts.title: Dimension and the Size of a Basis
concepts.summary: Any two bases of the same subspace have the same number of vectors, which is its dimension, so n + 1 vectors in R^n are always dependent and fewer than n never span it.

concepts.title: Coordinates Relative to a Basis
concepts.summary: Once a basis B is fixed, the coordinates of x relative to B are the unique weights that express x in that basis, and they change when the basis changes even though x itself does not.
prerequisites: Dimension and the Size of a Basis

concepts.title: The Vector Space Axioms
concepts.summary: A vector space is a set with an addition and a scalar multiplication satisfying the ten axioms, so polynomials of bounded degree, matrices and functions are vector spaces whose elements are not arrows.

concepts.title: Bases and Dimension in Abstract Spaces
concepts.summary: The subspace test, the basis definition and the dimension theorem use the same words in any vector space, so the polynomials of degree at most n have dimension n + 1 with basis 1, x, ..., x^n.

strands.strand: The Four Fundamental Subspaces and Rank

units.unit: The Four Fundamental Subspaces and Rank

concepts.title: The Column Space of a Matrix
concepts.summary: The column space of an m by n matrix A is the span of its columns, so it equals the set of b for which Ax = b is consistent and it is a subspace of R^m.

concepts.title: The Null Space of a Matrix
concepts.summary: The null space of A is the set of solutions of Ax = 0, a subspace of R^n whose dimension is the number of free variables left by row reduction, so it is nontrivial exactly when some column is not a pivot column.
prerequisites: The Column Space of a Matrix

topics.topic: Row Space and Left Null Space

concepts.title: The Row Space and the Rank
concepts.summary: The row space of A is the span of its rows, row operations leave it unchanged, and its dimension is the number of pivots, which is by definition the rank of A.

concepts.title: The Left Null Space
concepts.summary: The left null space of A consists of the vectors y with y^T A = 0, and it is the orthogonal complement of the column space inside R^m, of dimension m - r when A has rank r.
prerequisites: The Row Space and the Rank

concepts.title: Rank-Nullity
concepts.summary: Rank-nullity gives dim(column space) + dim(null space) = n for an m by n matrix, so a matrix with more columns than rows must have a nontrivial null space.

concepts.title: Rank Bounds and Their Consequences
concepts.summary: The rank of an m by n matrix satisfies r at most the smaller of m and n, and an n by n matrix is invertible exactly when r = n, so full rank is both necessary and sufficient for invertibility.

concepts.title: The Four Subspaces in One Picture
concepts.summary: For an m by n matrix of rank r, the column space and left null space sit inside R^m with dimensions r and m - r, while the null space and row space sit inside R^n with dimensions n - r and r.

concepts.title: The Linearity Conditions
concepts.summary: A map T from R^n to R^m is linear when it preserves sums and scalar multiples, equivalently when T(0) = 0 and T sends every linear combination to the matching combination of images, so a translation by a nonzero vector is never linear.

concepts.title: The Standard Matrix of a Transformation
concepts.summary: Every linear T from R^n to R^m equals multiplication by the unique matrix whose j-th column is T(ej), so once standard bases are fixed a linear map and a matrix are the same object.

concepts.title: Rotations, Reflections, and Scalings
concepts.summary: A rotation about the origin has an orthogonal matrix with determinant 1, a reflection has determinant -1, and a scaling multiplies lengths by its factor, so each family is read off its matrix.

concepts.title: Determinants as a Geometric Classifier
concepts.summary: The determinant of a linear map scales signed area or volume by that factor, so a zero determinant collapses the image to lower dimension while a negative one reverses orientation.

concepts.title: Kernel and Image as Subspaces
concepts.summary: The kernel of T is the set of inputs sent to zero and the image is the set of outputs actually attained, and both are subspaces, of the domain and the codomain respectively.

concepts.title: One-to-One and Onto in Matrix Terms
concepts.summary: A linear map is one-to-one exactly when its kernel is the zero subspace and onto exactly when its image is the whole codomain, which for T(x) = Ax means a pivot in every column and a pivot in every row respectively.

concepts.title: Rank-Nullity for Transformations
concepts.summary: For a linear map on a finite-dimensional domain, the dimension of the domain equals dim(kernel) + dim(image), so no linear map from R^3 to R^2 can be one-to-one.
prerequisites: One-to-One and Onto in Matrix Terms

concepts.title: The Change-of-Basis Matrix
concepts.summary: The change-of-basis matrix from B to C has the C-coordinates of the B basis vectors as its columns, and multiplying it by B-coordinates returns the C-coordinates of the same vector.

concepts.title: Similar Matrices Represent One Map
concepts.summary: Two matrices represent the same linear map in different bases exactly when they are similar, B = P^-1 A P for some invertible P, so similar matrices share determinant, trace, rank and eigenvalues.

prerequisites: The Four Fundamental Subspaces and Rank

concepts.title: Orthogonal Sets and Independence
concepts.summary: A set of nonzero vectors that are pairwise orthogonal is linearly independent, because dotting a zero combination with one member isolates that member as the only surviving term.

concepts.title: Orthonormal Bases and Their Coordinates
concepts.summary: An orthonormal basis consists of mutually orthogonal unit vectors, and then the coordinates of any vector are simply its dot products with the basis vectors, so no linear system has to be solved.

concepts.title: The Orthogonal Complement
concepts.summary: The orthogonal complement of a subspace W is the set of vectors orthogonal to every vector of W, which is itself a subspace and satisfies dim W + dim W complement = n inside R^n.

concepts.title: Unique Decomposition into Complements
concepts.summary: Every vector of R^n splits in exactly one way as a part in W plus a part in its orthogonal complement, and taking the complement twice returns W, so a subspace and its complement determine each other.

concepts.title: The Four Subspaces as Complement Pairs
concepts.summary: For any matrix A the null space of A is the orthogonal complement of the row space and the left null space is the orthogonal complement of the column space, which is what forces the dimension pairs r and n - r.

concepts.title: The Projection Formula
concepts.summary: For a subspace W with orthonormal basis u1 to uk, the projection of x onto W is the sum of (x.ui)ui, and the residual x minus that projection is orthogonal to every vector of W.

concepts.title: Projection Matrices
concepts.summary: Projection onto the column space of a matrix A with independent columns is multiplication by P = A(A^T A)^-1 A^T, and such a P satisfies P^2 = P and P^T = P.

concepts.title: The Least-Squares Problem
concepts.summary: When Ax = b has no solution, a least-squares solution minimises the length of Ax - b, which is the same as projecting b onto the column space of A.

concepts.title: When the Normal Equations Are Unique
concepts.summary: Least-squares solutions are exactly the solutions of the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b, which are always consistent, and the solution is unique exactly when the columns of A are linearly independent.

concepts.title: Fitting a Line by Least Squares
concepts.summary: A straight-line fit to data points (ti, bi) is the least-squares problem for the design matrix with columns of ones and ti, so the intercept and slope solve a 2 by 2 normal system.

concepts.title: Residuals and the Projection View
concepts.summary: The least-squares residual b - Ax is orthogonal to every column of A, so the fitted values are the projection of b onto the column space and the residual carries only what that space cannot represent.
prerequisites: Fitting a Line by Least Squares

concepts.title: The Gram-Schmidt Process
concepts.summary: Gram-Schmidt replaces each vector by its residual after subtracting its projections onto the previous orthonormal vectors, so the span of the first k vectors is unchanged at every step.

concepts.title: The QR Factorization
concepts.summary: When A has linearly independent columns, Gram-Schmidt gives A = QR with Q of orthonormal columns and R upper triangular with positive diagonal, so Ax = b becomes the triangular system Rx = Q^T b.

concepts.title: Cofactor Expansion
concepts.summary: The determinant expands along any row or column as a signed sum of entries times their minors, with the signs following the checkerboard pattern, so expanding along the row or column with the most zeros is cheapest.

concepts.title: Triangular Matrices and Elimination
concepts.summary: The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries, and during elimination a row replacement leaves the determinant unchanged while a swap multiplies it by -1 and a row scaling multiplies it by the same factor.

concepts.title: The Product Rule for Determinants
concepts.summary: For square matrices of the same size the determinant is multiplicative, det(AB) = det(A)det(B), so an invertible A has det(A^-1) = 1/det(A) and det(A^k) = det(A)^k.

concepts.title: Singularity and the Determinant
concepts.summary: A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero, because elimination produces a zero pivot exactly when the determinant vanishes, and a matrix and its transpose share one determinant.

concepts.title: Determinants as Volume
concepts.summary: The absolute value of the determinant of a square matrix is the volume of the parallelepiped its columns span, so a zero determinant means the columns are dependent and that volume has collapsed.

concepts.title: Cramer's Rule and the Adjugate
concepts.summary: Cramer's rule writes each component of the solution of Ax = b as a ratio of determinants, and the adjugate formula A^-1 = adj(A)/det(A) restates the same fact, both requiring det(A) nonzero.

concepts.title: The Eigenvalue Equation
concepts.summary: A nonzero v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue lambda when Av = lambda v, and lambda is an eigenvalue exactly when A - lambda I is singular, so the eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic polynomial.

concepts.title: Eigenspaces and Multiplicity
concepts.summary: The eigenvectors for a fixed eigenvalue together with the zero vector form the eigenspace, the null space of A - lambda I, so its dimension is the geometric multiplicity and never exceeds the algebraic multiplicity of the root.

concepts.title: Eigenvalues from Trace and Determinant
concepts.summary: For a 2 by 2 matrix the two eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant, which often recovers them from one quadratic without expanding the characteristic polynomial in full.

concepts.title: The Diagonalization Criterion
concepts.summary: An n by n matrix is diagonalisable exactly when it has n linearly independent eigenvectors, and then A = PDP^-1 with D the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues and P the matrix of eigenvectors.

concepts.title: Distinct Eigenvalues and Independence
concepts.summary: Eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so a matrix with n distinct eigenvalues is diagonalisable, while a repeated eigenvalue may still supply enough eigenvectors or may not.

concepts.title: Powers from Diagonalization
concepts.summary: Once A = PDP^-1 holds, every power is A^k = PD^kP^-1, so diagonalisation turns repeated application of A into raising each eigenvalue to the k-th power.

concepts.title: Complex Eigenvalues in Conjugate Pairs
concepts.summary: A real matrix can have nonreal eigenvalues, and they occur in conjugate pairs with conjugate eigenvectors, so a 2 by 2 rotation by theta has eigenvalues cos theta plus or minus i sin theta.

concepts.title: Rotation and Scaling from Complex Eigenvalues
concepts.summary: A real 2 by 2 matrix with complex eigenvalues is similar to a rotation combined with a scaling by the modulus of the eigenvalue, which is why its orbits spiral instead of lying along invariant lines.

concepts.title: Markov Matrices and Steady States
concepts.summary: A Markov matrix has nonnegative entries with every column summing to 1, so 1 is always an eigenvalue and a steady state is a probability eigenvector for it.

concepts.title: Convergence to the Steady State
concepts.summary: If some power of a Markov matrix has all positive entries then the iterates converge to the steady state from every starting distribution, because all other eigenvalues have modulus strictly below 1.

strands.strand: Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Theorem

units.unit: Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Theorem

concepts.title: Orthogonal Diagonalization of Symmetric Matrices
concepts.summary: A real matrix is symmetric exactly when it equals QDQ^T with Q orthogonal and D real diagonal, so every symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors.

concepts.title: Orthogonality of Eigenvectors
concepts.summary: Eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix that belong to different eigenvalues are orthogonal, which is the step that lets each eigenspace be orthonormalised separately and still combine into one orthonormal eigenbasis.

concepts.title: The Quadratic Form of a Matrix
concepts.summary: A quadratic form is x^T A x for a symmetric A, and replacing A by its symmetric part leaves every value unchanged, so every quadratic form may be written with a symmetric matrix without loss.

concepts.title: Diagonalizing a Quadratic Form
concepts.summary: Substituting x = Qy with Q the orthogonal eigenvector matrix turns x^T A x into a weighted sum of squares of the y coordinates, so the eigenvalues are the coefficients in the principal-axis description.
prerequisites: The Quadratic Form of a Matrix

concepts.title: The Positive-Definite Test
concepts.summary: A symmetric matrix is positive definite when x^T A x is positive for every nonzero x, which holds exactly when all its eigenvalues are positive, and then it factors as R^T R with R invertible.

concepts.title: Sylvester's Criterion
concepts.summary: Sylvester's criterion says a symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when every leading principal minor is positive, so definiteness is checked from the elimination pivots without computing eigenvalues.

concepts.title: Singular Values of a Matrix
concepts.summary: The singular values of A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of A^T A, which are nonnegative because A^T A is symmetric positive semidefinite, and the right singular vectors are its orthonormal eigenvectors.

concepts.title: The SVD Factorization
concepts.summary: Every m by n matrix factors as A = U Sigma V^T with U and V orthogonal and Sigma diagonal with nonnegative entries in decreasing order, and the rank of A is the number of positive singular values.

topics.topic: Geometry and Subspaces of the SVD

concepts.title: The SVD as Rotate-Scale-Rotate
concepts.summary: The SVD sends each right singular vector vi to the scaled left singular vector sigma_i ui, so it maps the unit sphere to an ellipsoid whose semi-axis lengths are the singular values and generalises diagonalisation to non-square matrices.

concepts.title: Singular Vectors as Subspace Bases
concepts.summary: The right singular vectors with positive singular values form an orthonormal basis of the row space, the matching left singular vectors one of the column space, and the remaining vectors span the two null spaces.

concepts.title: The Best Rank-k Approximation
concepts.summary: Truncating the SVD after its k largest singular values gives the matrix of rank at most k nearest to A in both the spectral and Frobenius norms, which is the Eckart-Young theorem.

concepts.title: Pseudoinverse and Condition Number
concepts.summary: The pseudoinverse V Sigma^+ U^T solves the least-squares problem for rank-deficient A, and the ratio of largest to smallest positive singular value measures how strongly small data errors are amplified.

prerequisites: Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Theorem
